content.thinking:
I'm starting the postmortem by laying out the facts. The symptom is that account pages failed for many shoppers, with no count given yet. I'm tracing the causal chain, beginning with the user-facing errors and then the ZeroDivisionError raised in spend_summary.py at line 47.

I'm checking the earlier changes next. The monthly-spend feature doesn't look like the trigger, since turning it off didn't stop the errors, and no deploys came back in the window.

I'm checking whether the new renderer path explains the ZeroDivisionError. Per the F1 reading, it calls the monthly average, which divides by the count of purchases this month, and that count is zero for shoppers who haven't bought anything this month. That reading is unverified, though, since the monthly-spend flag being off didn't stop the errors, so I can't yet tie the divisor to the failing requests.

I'm now settling the last link in the chain: the new renderer's path computes a monthly per-item spend figure that divides by the shopper's purchases this month, which fails for anyone who hasn't bought anything this month. Since the account pages that hit line 47 were being served by that new renderer, I'm checking whether each failed request becomes a failed page as well.

Now I'm checking the timing on the legacy and new renderers: the legacy one served essentially everything up to 18:14, and the new one took over after that, peaking at 18:16. I'm also setting aside a ClientDisconnected warning that shows up a few times between 18:14 and 18:18, since it doesn't bear on the failures.

I'm ruling out the monthly-spend feature as the trigger, since switching it back off left the service at incident level, and I'm noting that no deploy came back in the day before onset. I'm now listing the contributing factors.

I'm working out the first contributing factor: nobody was paged, since the alert never linked to an on-call incident. A person being notified at the alert could have taken over alongside Argus, so the lack of a page held before the incident and is worth recording on its own.

I'm weighing the two flags that were switched together at the same instant, which left the logs unable to separate which one caused the errors. That cost a refuted mitigation before the right one was found. Had they been changed separately, the errors could have been tied to the fallback directly and reverted first, shortening the incident.

I'm noting that the new test would fail against current code, but the existing tests never cover the case where a shopper has no purchases this month. I'm weighing whether to add a check for that before the change went out, and I'm drafting a prevention item to put one in place for every change like it.

I'm noting a third contributing factor: the flag went from mostly on to fully off within a single minute, so every user was moved onto the new path at once with no gradual rollout. Had it been phased in to a small share with error watching, the damage would have stayed contained.

I'm setting the action items against the contributing factors: the staggered flag changes, a check on the new path's empty-month case before any switch, and a staged rollout instead of moving everyone at once. I'm also noting that the missing on-call link on the error-rate alert needs its own item.

I'm weighing whether to add a flag-lock on legacy-checkout-fallback so it can't be switched off until the fix is merged, since turning it off again would bring the failures back.

I'm settling the action items: a process rule that flag changes on io-shop go one at a time with a watch period, a test covering shoppers with no purchases this month before a traffic-moving flag switch, and a staged rollout that halts on rising error rates. The HighErrorRate alert also needs an on-call link, and legacy-checkout-fallback should stay locked on until the fix is merged.

I'm working out how the root cause reads in plain terms: with the fallback flag off, account pages go through the new renderer, and the spend summary there divides by the count of this month's purchases, which is zero for shoppers who haven't bought anything yet this month.

I'm settling how the root cause reads for the review: the account-page path served once the flag was off runs render_spend_summary, which sends requests with use_monthly_summary on to average_spend_per_item_this_month, the function the error names.

I'm going through the lead effects next: the investigation weighed the monthly-spend lead as unverified and went after the wrong flag first, and only after that was refuted did it turn to the one that was right, so the lead changed nothing about what was done first. I'm also noting what went well, starting with the Investigator Agent reading the flag history and log lines and naming both flags as candidates.

I'm going through what went wrong: the lead pointed at the right flag before any action, but the first revert went to monthly-spend-feature, which ranked higher, so a refuted attempt came before the one that confirmed the fix. I'm also noting that nobody was paged.

I'm checking which assumptions the write-up rests on. The link between the fallback flag and the spend-summary path is inferred from timing and from the revert that stopped the errors, since the renderer code itself wasn't in the record. I'm also noting that the path through the monthly per-item average is an inference too, not something I've seen directly.

I'm checking the chain's supporting citations now, tying each step to its timeline rows and log lines. The monthly-spend feature and the deploy history both drop out as triggers, since switching the feature back off didn't clear the incident and no deploy landed the day before onset. Healthy readings before the incident are noted as well.

I'm checking the postmortem's action items against the contributing factors, making sure each one traces back to a specific cause in the record.

action_items.item: Require io-shop feature flags to be changed one at a time, with a watch period on the error rate before the next flag is changed.
Before any io-shop flag that moves traffic onto a different code path is changed, require that path's tests to pass for ordinary shopper cases, including a shopper with no purchases this month.
Roll out io-shop flag changes to a small share of traffic first, and halt them automatically when the error rate rises.
Link the HighErrorRate alert on io-shop to an on-call page so that a person is paged when it fires.
Lock legacy-checkout-fallback on until the proposed fix in PR #433 is merged, so it cannot be switched off again with the fault in place.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' account page requests failed: the service's own warning on the account page error rate rose from its usual level and stayed high.
Account page requests raised ZeroDivisionError at the line named in src/io_shop/spend_summary.py, and each such request failed.

ruled_out.what: monthly-spend-feature, switched on by the same admin at the same instant: switching it back off left the service at the incident's level, and the action was judged refuted.
A deploy: none came back for the day before the onset.

causal_chain.step: Those requests went down a different path because legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off at {P1.1}. Account pages moved from the legacy renderer to the new one: the logs show the flag mostly off in the minute of the change and fully off in every minute after it, and the new renderer serving the pages from then on. Turning the flag back on brought the service back.

On the path served once the flag was off, the spend summary works out a monthly spend-per-item figure that divides by the number of the shopper's purchases this month, and that fails for any shopper who has bought nothing this month.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching off an old fallback setting sent shoppers' account pages through newer code that most likely fails when it works out a monthly spend-per-item figure for shoppers who have bought nothing yet this month.

contributing_factors.factor: The same admin switched legacy-checkout-fallback and monthly-spend-feature at the same instant, so the logs could not tell which change caused the failures.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: With the flags changed one at a time, the failures would have lined up with legacy-checkout-fallback alone. That flag could then have been reverted first, without the refuted revert of monthly-spend-feature, and the incident would have been shorter.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Before legacy-checkout-fallback was switched off, no check was seen that the account-page path it moves traffic onto handles a shopper with no purchases this month. Code-Fix reports that the test file's own fixture calls that the ordinary case.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A test of that path with an idle-this-month shopper would have raised the error before the flag change, and the flag would not have been switched off with the fault in place.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No staged rollout of the flag change was seen: legacy-checkout-fallback went from on to off for nearly all evaluations within the minute it changed, and for all of them from the next minute.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Moving a small share of account pages first and stopping when errors rose would have kept the failures to that share, not most of the traffic.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

lead_effects.effect: It did not change what was done: Argus reverted monthly-spend-feature first and turned to legacy-checkout-fallback only as the next candidate once that revert was refuted, though the lead turned out to be right.

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent read the flag provider's history and the log lines, and listed both flags that changed as candidate causes.
The Mitigation Agent put monthly-spend-feature back on once reverting it had not helped, so no change that did nothing was left in place.
The Mitigation Agent reverted legacy-checkout-fallback, and that brought the service back.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix, with tests, as a draft pull request for a person to review.

went_wrong: The lead in the thread named the right flag before any action was taken, but the investigation weighed it as unverified and reverted monthly-spend-feature first, so a refuted action came before the one that worked.
The alert paged nobody: no on-call incident was linked to it.

input.root_cause: Once legacy-checkout-fallback was off, account pages were served by a path that reaches the spend summary. According to Code-Fix's reading, `render_spend_summary` sends requests that have `use_monthly_summary` on to `average_spend_per_item_this_month` in `src/io_shop/spend_summary.py`, and at line {F1.1} that function divides the month's total by `len(bought_this_month)`. That list is empty for any shopper who has bought nothing this month, so the request raises ZeroDivisionError, and `serve_account_page` turns the error into a failed page.
input.still_at_risk: If legacy-checkout-fallback is switched off again, account pages for shoppers who have bought nothing this month could fail the same way again.
input.symptom: Account pages failed for many shoppers
